name: Horizontal Block Exemption Regulations (R&D 2023/1066 and specialisation 2023/1067)
impact_assessment: No published impact assessment report; evaluation SWD(2021) 103
evidence_rating: very thin: Commission evaluation of the predecessor rules (qualitative) and theory; no empirical study of effects on R&D cooperation or innovation
summary: These two Commission regulations let competitors cooperate on research and on specialised production without breaching EU competition law if they stay below market-share limits. The Commission's 2021 evaluation of the previous rules found them useful but outdated, and could not measure how much they saved companies. No study has measured whether the block exemptions increase research cooperation or innovation.

indicators.objective: Commission regulations adopted without a legislative proposal or financial statement, so there are no LFS indicators; the 2023 rules replaced Regulations 1217/2010 and 1218/2010 after an evaluation (SWD(2021) 103) and an impact assessment phase with five support studies whose report was not found on EUR-Lex

indicators.indicator: Firms and authorities find the block exemptions clear and usable
indicators.evidence: 2021 evaluation: rules still relevant and made economically desirable cooperation easier, but some conditions seen as too strict or unclear; need to reflect digitalisation and sustainability. The 2023 revision responds to this; no ex-post check of the new rules yet (they expire in 2035).

indicators.indicator: Self-assessment costs saved compared with no block exemption
indicators.evidence: Evaluation could not quantify savings: most stakeholders did not know whether costs had changed; few gave estimates.

indicators.indicator: More pro-competitive R&D cooperation and innovation
indicators.evidence: No empirical study found of the block exemption's effect on R&D cooperation or innovation; theory suggests the 25% market-share safe harbour is not clearly justified.

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Evaluation of the Horizontal Block Exemption Regulations (R&D and Specialisation) and the Horizontal Guidelines, SWD(2021) 103
literature.title: Evaluation of the Horizontal Block Exemption Regulations (R&D and Specialisation) and the Horizontal Guidelines
literature.method: evaluation (public consultation 2019-20, external evaluation study, NCA survey)
literature.headline: HBERs and Guidelines made economically desirable cooperation easier and gave legal certainty, but some rules unduly strict or unclear and outdated for digitalisation and sustainability; compliance-cost savings could not be quantified
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's evaluation found the old rules useful for firms that cooperate on research or production, but in need of updating and unable to put a number on the money saved.

literature.citation: European Commission (DG Competition) (2023), Explanatory note on the 2023 Horizontal Block Exemption Regulations, DG Competition
literature.title: Explanatory note on the 2023 Horizontal Block Exemption Regulations
literature.headline: Revision addresses issues found in the evaluation, informed by an impact assessment phase with stakeholder workshops and five support studies; changes to market-share calculation, innovation competition and SME usability
literature.summary_plain: The Commission explains that the 2023 rules fix problems found in the evaluation, but publishes no forecast of their economic effect.

literature.citation: Ruble & Versaevel (2014), Market shares, R&D agreements, and the EU block exemption, International Review of Law and Economics 37: 15-25
literature.title: Market shares, R&D agreements, and the EU block exemption
literature.venue: International Review of Law and Economics 37: 15-25
literature.headline: Incentives to innovate under cooperation depend on several effects; an 'outsider effect' can raise R&D when combined market share is high, so theory does not support limiting the exemption to low market shares
literature.summary_plain: A theory paper argues that the market-share cap in the R&D block exemption may exclude cooperation that would actually boost innovation.
